learn.hook: Imagine sorting your class only by height. Tall friends would be 'related'. Early plant classification made a similar mistake.
points: Artificial systems (e.g. Linnaeus) used only a few characters such as habit, colour, number and shape of leaves, or the androecium. They gave equal weight to vegetative and sexual characters, which is unacceptable because vegetative characters are easily affected by the environment.
Natural systems (e.g. Bentham and Hooker) are based on natural affinities and use many characters: external features and internal ones such as ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology and phytochemistry.
Phylogenetic systems are based on evolutionary relationships; they assume members of a taxon share a common ancestor.
Numerical taxonomy uses computers: all observable characters are coded as numbers and given equal importance, so hundreds of characters can be handled.
Cytotaxonomy uses chromosome number, structure and behaviour; chemotaxonomy uses the plant's chemical constituents.

example.q: Two plant groups look alike, but one has 2n = 14 and the other 2n = 24, and their alkaloids differ. Which branches of taxonomy use these clues?
steps: Chromosome number is cytological information: cytotaxonomy.
Chemical constituents such as alkaloids: chemotaxonomy.

learn.reallife: Indian scientists at institutes such as the Botanical Survey of India now combine DNA, chromosome and chemical data to classify medicinal plants used in Ayurveda.

quiz.explain: Natural systems use many characters; a single character like stamen number is typical of artificial systems.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why did scientists stop classifying plants just by their leaves?' Explain the different classification systems!
teach.praise: Tweet! From a few characters to evolution and computers. Classification got smarter!
teach.nudge: Good! What was wrong with artificial systems, and what do phylogenetic systems use?

learn.hook: The agar in your school lab petri dish and in some ice creams comes from red seaweed off the coast. Algae are quietly everywhere.
points: Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and mostly aquatic. Forms range from unicellular (Chlamydomonas) and colonial (Volvox) to filamentous (Ulothrix, Spirogyra) and massive marine kelps.
Vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation; asexual reproduction is by spores, most commonly flagellated zoospores.

Sexual reproduction: isogamy (gametes similar in size; flagellated in Chlamydomonas, non-flagellated in Spirogyra), anisogamy (gametes dissimilar in size, e.g. species of Eudorina), oogamy (large non-motile female and small motile male gamete, e.g. Volvox, Fucus).
Algae carry out at least half of the total CO₂ fixation on Earth and are primary producers in aquatic food chains.

Uses: about 70 marine species are eaten, e.g. Porphyra, Laminaria, Sargassum. Algin (brown algae) and carrageen (red algae) are used commercially; agar (Gelidium, Gracilaria) is used to grow microbes and in jellies and ice creams; Chlorella, rich in protein, is a food supplement even for space travellers.

example.q: In an alga, a large non-motile egg is fertilised by a small motile male gamete. Name the type of sexual reproduction and give two examples.
steps: Gametes differ in size and motility.
Large non-motile female with small motile male is oogamy.

learn.reallife: Seaweed farming of Gracilaria and Kappaphycus along Tamil Nadu's Ramanathapuram coast gives coastal women's groups an income from agar and carrageenan.

games.title: Type of sexual reproduction
items: Gametes dissimilar in size, both motile

quiz.q: Volvox is an example of which algal form?
quiz.explain: Volvox is a colonial green alga.

quiz.q: The most common asexual spores in algae are:
quiz.explain: Algae usually reproduce asexually by flagellated zoospores.

quiz.q: Fusion of two gametes that are similar in size is called:
quiz.explain: Iso- means equal.

quiz.q: Agar is obtained from:
quiz.explain: Agar comes from the red algae Gelidium and Gracilaria.
quiz.mistake: Confuses agar with algin from brown algae

quiz.q: Algae carry out roughly what share of Earth's total CO₂ fixation by photosynthesis?
quiz.explain: Algae fix at least half of all CO₂ fixed on Earth.

quiz.q: Which alga is used as a protein-rich food supplement, even by space travellers?
quiz.explain: Chlorella is unicellular and rich in proteins.
quiz.mistake: Picks a seaweed eaten as food

quiz.q: Spirogyra shows isogamy with gametes that are:
quiz.explain: Spirogyra's isogamous gametes are non-flagellated (non-motile).
quiz.mistake: Assumes all algal gametes are flagellated

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Algae are called primary producers in aquatic ecosystems. Reason (R): Algae are photosynthetic and form the base of aquatic food chains.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; making food by photosynthesis for the food chain is what primary producer means.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect photosynthesis with being a producer

teach.ask: Gappu thinks seaweed is just slimy rubbish. Show him how algae reproduce and why they matter to us!
teach.praise: Chirp! Three kinds of sexual reproduction and agar for ice cream. Seaweed is cool!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the three types of sexual reproduction, and name one useful algal product.

topics.title: Classes of algae: green, brown and red

learn.hook: Why are some seaweeds red even when they live deep under the sea? The answer lies in a pigment that catches the light that reaches the depths.
points: Chlorophyceae (green algae): chlorophyll a and b; chloroplasts of many shapes; pyrenoids store protein and starch; food stored as starch (and oil); cell wall of inner cellulose and outer pectose; 2 to 8 equal apical flagella. Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara.

Phaeophyceae (brown algae): mainly marine; chlorophyll a and c, carotenoids and xanthophylls (fucoxanthin); food as laminarin or mannitol; cellulose wall covered by gelatinous algin; body has holdfast, stipe and frond; 2 unequal lateral flagella. Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus.

Rhodophyceae (red algae): pigment r-phycoerythrin with chlorophyll a and d; mostly marine, near the surface and at great depths; food as floridean starch (like amylopectin and glycogen); wall of cellulose, pectin and polysulphate esters; no flagella. Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium.
Red algae reproduce sexually by oogamy with complex post-fertilisation development; asexual spores are non-motile.

example.q: An alga has chlorophyll a and c, stores mannitol, and has a holdfast and frond. Classify it.
steps: Chlorophyll c and mannitol are brown-algal features.
Holdfast, stipe and frond describe brown algae.

learn.reallife: Sargassum washes up on the Gulf of Mannar beaches, and Porphyra is a sea vegetable widely eaten in East Asia.

games.title: Algal structure to role
pairs: Attaches a brown alga to the substratum
Gelatinous coating on brown algal walls

quiz.q: Floridean starch is the stored food of:
quiz.explain: Red algae store floridean starch, similar to amylopectin and glycogen.

quiz.q: The main pigment that gives red algae their colour is:
quiz.explain: r-phycoerythrin gives red algae their colour.

quiz.q: Brown algae store food as:
quiz.explain: Laminarin and mannitol are brown-algal reserves.

quiz.q: Pyrenoids in green algae contain:
quiz.explain: Pyrenoids store protein besides starch.

quiz.q: Which class has chlorophyll a and c along with fucoxanthin?
quiz.explain: Fucoxanthin and chlorophyll c are characteristic of brown algae.
quiz.mistake: Confuses brown and red algal pigments

quiz.q: In brown algae, the leaf-like photosynthetic part of the body is the:
quiz.explain: Holdfast attaches, stipe is the stalk, and the frond photosynthesises.

quiz.q: Which algal class lacks flagella altogether?
quiz.explain: Red algae have no flagella; green algae have 2–8 equal apical flagella and brown algae have 2 unequal lateral flagella.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all algae have flagellated stages

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Red algae can grow at great depths in the sea. Reason (R): Red algae have r-phycoerythrin, which absorbs the light that penetrates to those depths.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; their pigment lets them use the light available deep down, explaining their depth range.
quiz.mistake: Does not link pigment to habitat

teach.ask: Gappu holds a green, a brown and a red seaweed. Help him tell the three classes apart by pigment and stored food!
teach.praise: Tweet! Starch for green, laminarin for brown, floridean starch for red. Colour-coded biology!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the stored food and special pigment of each class?

topics.title: Bryophytes: amphibians of the plant kingdom

learn.hook: After the monsoon, a green velvet covers old walls in Kerala. These mosses need land to live on but water to have babies, just like frogs.
points: Bryophytes live in soil but depend on water for sexual reproduction, so they are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom. They grow in damp, humid, shaded places and help plant succession on bare rocks and soil.
The plant body is thallus-like, prostrate or erect, attached by rhizoids. It has no true roots, stems or leaves. The main plant body is the haploid gametophyte.
Sex organs are multicellular. The antheridium produces biflagellate antherozoids; the flask-shaped archegonium has a single egg. Antherozoids swim through water to reach the egg.

The zygote forms a multicellular sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) that stays attached to the gametophyte and depends on it for food. Some sporophyte cells undergo meiosis to form haploid spores, which grow into new gametophytes.

Uses: food for herbivorous mammals and birds; Sphagnum gives peat, used as fuel and as packing material for living material because it holds water. Mosses with lichens are first colonisers of rocks, and moss mats reduce soil erosion.

example.q: Why does a moss plant fail to produce a sporophyte in a long dry spell?
steps: Antherozoids are flagellated and must swim to the archegonium.
Without water, they cannot reach the egg.
No fertilisation means no zygote, so no sporophyte.
example.answer: Fertilisation needs water; without it no zygote or sporophyte forms.

learn.reallife: Sphagnum peat moss is used by plant nurseries to pack and transport living saplings because it holds water so well.

games.title: Bryophyte life cycle

Sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) grows on the gametophyte
Meiosis in capsule forms haploid spores

It stays attached and derives nourishment.

Peat is used as fuel and packing material.
Spores in bryophytes are formed by mitosis.
They are formed by meiosis (reduction division).

quiz.q: Bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom because they:
quiz.explain: Water is needed for antherozoids to reach the egg.
options: Live on land but need water for sexual reproduction

quiz.q: The dominant, independent phase in bryophytes is the:
quiz.explain: The main plant body is the haploid gametophyte.

quiz.q: The sporophyte of a bryophyte is differentiated into:
quiz.explain: Foot anchors, seta is a stalk, capsule bears spores.

quiz.q: The female sex organ of a bryophyte is the:
quiz.explain: The flask-shaped archegonium holds a single egg.

quiz.q: Bryophytes are important in plant succession because they:
quiz.explain: Mosses and lichens are early colonisers that break down rock.
options: Colonise bare rocks along with lichens and help form soil

quiz.q: Why is Sphagnum used to pack living plant material for transport?
quiz.explain: Sphagnum holds lots of water, keeping material moist.
options: It has a high water-holding capacity

quiz.q: In bryophytes, spores are produced by:
quiz.explain: Spore mother cells in the capsule undergo reduction division.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The sporophyte of a moss is free-living and independent of the gametophyte. Reason (R): The moss sporophyte stays attached to the photosynthetic gametophyte and gets nourishment from it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: the moss sporophyte cannot live on its own. R is true: it stays attached to the gametophyte and depends on it for food, which is exactly why it is not free-living.
quiz.mistake: Judges the assertion true just because the reason is a correct fact

teach.ask: Gappu sees moss on a wet wall and asks: 'Why does it love water so much, and which part is the real plant?' Explain!
teach.praise: Chirp! A haploid gametophyte that needs water for its swimmers. Amphibian plants!
teach.nudge: Good! Which generation is the main plant, and why is water needed?

learn.hook: Marchantia carries tiny 'cups' full of green buds that splash away in rain drops to start new plants.
points: Liverworts grow in moist shady places such as stream banks, marshy ground, damp soil, tree bark and deep woods. The thalloid body of Marchantia is dorsiventral and closely pressed to the ground; leafy liverworts have tiny leaf-like parts in two rows.
Liverworts reproduce asexually by fragmentation or by gemmae: green, multicellular asexual buds formed in gemma cups on the thallus. Gemmae detach and grow into new plants.
In liverworts, male and female sex organs may be on the same or different thalli; the sporophyte has foot, seta and capsule, and spores form after meiosis.

Mosses: the gametophyte has two stages. The protonema grows directly from a spore and is creeping, green, branched and often filamentous. The leafy stage grows from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud, with upright axes bearing spirally arranged leaves and multicellular branched rhizoids; it bears the sex organs.

Mosses reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation and budding of the secondary protonema. Their sporophyte is more elaborate than in liverworts, with an elaborate mechanism of spore dispersal. Examples: Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum.

example.q: A student sees a green filament growing from a moss spore. What is it and what will it give rise to?
steps: A creeping green filament growing directly from a spore is the protonema.
Lateral buds on it grow into the leafy stage that bears sex organs.
example.answer: Protonema; it gives rise to the leafy gametophyte stage.

learn.reallife: Polytrichum and Funaria carpet Himalayan slopes in Darjeeling and Sikkim, holding soil during heavy rains.

quiz.q: Gemmae in Marchantia are:
quiz.explain: Gemmae form in gemma cups and grow into new thalli.

quiz.q: The first stage of a moss gametophyte, developing directly from a spore, is the:
quiz.explain: The protonema is creeping, green, branched and filamentous.
quiz.mistake: Confuses protonema with the fern prothallus

quiz.q: Rhizoids in mosses are:
quiz.explain: Moss rhizoids are multicellular and branched.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bryophyte rhizoids are true roots

quiz.q: In mosses, the sex organs are borne on the:
quiz.explain: Antheridia and archegonia form at the apex of the leafy shoots.
quiz.mistake: Places sex organs on the protonema

quiz.q: Which is a liverwort?
quiz.explain: Marchantia is a thalloid liverwort; the others are mosses.

quiz.q: Compared with liverworts, the sporophyte of mosses is:
quiz.explain: Moss sporophytes are more elaborate and have elaborate spore dispersal.

quiz.q: The thallus of Marchantia is:
quiz.explain: Marchantia's thallus lies flat and is dorsiventral.
options: Dorsiventral and closely appressed to the substrate

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In mosses, the leafy stage develops from the secondary protonema. Reason (R): The leafy stage arises as a lateral bud on the protonema.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true, and R describes how the leafy stage arises from the protonema.
quiz.mistake: Misses that R explains the origin

teach.ask: Gappu found two little green plants: one flat with tiny cups, one upright and leafy. Teach him liverworts vs mosses!
teach.praise: Tweet! Flat with cups is a liverwort; protonema then leafy shoots is a moss!
teach.nudge: Nice! What are gemmae, and what are the two stages of a moss gametophyte?

topics.title: Pteridophytes: the first vascular land plants

learn.hook: The lacy ferns in Ooty's gardens were the first plants to build 'plumbing pipes'. That's why they could stand taller than mosses.
points: Pteridophytes (horsetails and ferns) are the first terrestrial plants with vascular tissues, xylem and phloem. They mostly grow in cool, damp, shady places.
The main plant body is the diploid sporophyte with true roots, stems and leaves. Leaves may be small (microphylls, as in Selaginella) or large (macrophylls, as in ferns).
Sporangia are borne on leaf-like sporophylls. In some, sporophylls form compact strobili or cones (Selaginella, Equisetum). Spore mother cells undergo meiosis to form spores.
Spores grow into a small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic thalloid gametophyte called the prothallus, which needs cool, damp, shady places.
The prothallus bears antheridia and archegonia; water is needed for antherozoids to reach the egg. The zygote grows into the well-differentiated sporophyte.

example.q: Fern spores on a dry concrete wall do not produce new ferns, but on wet soil near a stream they do. Explain.
steps: Spores grow into the prothallus, which needs cool, damp, shady places.
Fertilisation on the prothallus also needs water for antherozoids to swim.
example.answer: The prothallus and fertilisation both need moist conditions.

learn.reallife: Ferns like Adiantum (maidenhair fern) are popular ornamental plants in Indian homes and hill-station gardens.

games.title: Pteridophyte facts
items: Pteridophytes were the first land plants with xylem and phloem.
They are the first vascular terrestrial plants.
The main plant body of a fern is the gametophyte.
Water is not needed for fertilisation in pteridophytes.
Antherozoids need water to reach the egg.
Spores of pteridophytes are formed by meiosis.

quiz.q: Pteridophytes were the first terrestrial plants to have:
quiz.explain: Xylem and phloem first appear in pteridophytes.

quiz.q: The gametophyte of a fern is called the:
quiz.explain: The fern gametophyte is the prothallus.
quiz.mistake: Confuses prothallus with the moss protonema

quiz.q: In pteridophytes, the main plant body is:
quiz.explain: The sporophyte is dominant and well differentiated.
options: A diploid sporophyte with true roots, stems and leaves

quiz.q: Selaginella has small leaves called:
quiz.explain: Selaginella has microphylls; ferns have macrophylls.

quiz.q: Leaf-like structures that bear sporangia are called:
quiz.explain: Sporophylls subtend the sporangia; a cluster of sporophylls forms a strobilus.

quiz.q: Which pteridophytes have sporophylls in compact strobili?
quiz.explain: Selaginella and Equisetum have compact cones.

quiz.q: Why are pteridophytes mostly restricted to damp, shady places?
quiz.explain: The free-living prothallus and water-dependent fertilisation limit them to moist places.
options: The prothallus and fertilisation need moisture
Their seeds need water to germinate

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Pteridophytes could grow taller than bryophytes. Reason (R): Pteridophytes were the first plants to produce seeds.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true: xylem and phloem let pteridophytes carry water and food over longer distances and support a bigger body. R is false: pteridophytes reproduce by spores; seeds first appear in gymnosperms.
quiz.mistake: Accepts the reason without checking it against the facts

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Ferns and mosses both like water, so what's the big difference?' Explain pteridophytes to him!
teach.praise: Chirp! Ferns have pipes and a big sporophyte, but still a tiny prothallus that needs water!
teach.nudge: Good! What tissues do ferns have that mosses lack, and what is the prothallus?

learn.hook: Selaginella makes two sizes of spores. That small step, keeping the female spore at home, set plants on the road to seeds.
points: Most pteridophytes are homosporous: they produce one kind of spore.
Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous: they produce large megaspores and small microspores, which grow into female and male gametophytes.
In heterosporous forms, the female gametophyte stays on the parent sporophyte for some time and the embryo develops inside it. This is a precursor to the seed habit, an important step in evolution.
Classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum) and Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum).
Uses: medicinal purposes, as soil binders, and as ornamentals.

example.q: Why is heterospory in Selaginella considered a step towards the seed habit?
steps: Megaspores and microspores form female and male gametophytes.
The female gametophyte is retained on the parent sporophyte.
The zygote develops into an embryo within it, as happens inside a seed.
example.answer: Retention of the female gametophyte and development of the embryo on the parent is a precursor to seeds.

learn.reallife: Pteris and Adiantum ferns grow on the walls of old forts in Rajasthan and the Western Ghats, and many ferns help bind soil on slopes.

items.text: Plants producing two kinds of spores are ___.
Heterospory is a precursor to the ___ habit.

quiz.q: Which pteridophyte is heterosporous?
quiz.explain: Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous; most ferns are homosporous.

quiz.q: Equisetum belongs to class:
quiz.explain: Equisetum (horsetail) is a sphenopsid.

quiz.q: Most pteridophytes are:
quiz.explain: The majority produce a single kind of spore.

quiz.q: A microspore of Selaginella develops into a:
quiz.explain: Microspores give male gametophytes; megaspores give female gametophytes.

quiz.q: Which event is regarded as a precursor to the seed habit?
quiz.explain: In heterosporous forms the embryo develops within the retained female gametophyte, like in a seed.
options: Retention of the female gametophyte and development of the embryo on the parent sporophyte

quiz.q: Dryopteris, Pteris and Adiantum belong to:
quiz.explain: These ferns are placed in Pteropsida.

quiz.q: Which is a use of pteridophytes?
quiz.explain: Pteridophytes are used as soil binders, ornamentals and in medicine.
quiz.mistake: Gives a use of algae or mosses

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Salvinia is a heterosporous pteridophyte. Reason (R): Salvinia produces only one kind of spore.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Salvinia produces megaspores and microspores, so A is true and R is false.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did plants go from spores to seeds?' Tell him about heterospory and the four classes of pteridophytes!
teach.praise: Tweet! Two sizes of spores, and the female one stays home. Seeds are on the way!
teach.nudge: Good! Which plants make two kinds of spores, and why is that important?

topics.title: Gymnosperms: naked seeds, roots and leaves

learn.hook: The tallest trees on Earth, the redwoods, are gymnosperms. So is the pine whose resin makes turpentine, and the cycad in your local park.
points: Gymnosperms (gymnos = naked, sperma = seeds) have ovules not enclosed by an ovary wall, before or after fertilisation.
They include medium to tall trees and shrubs. Sequoia, the giant redwood, is one of the tallest tree species.
Roots are generally tap roots. Pinus has mycorrhizal roots (fungal association); Cycas has small coralloid roots associated with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria.
Stems may be unbranched (Cycas) or branched (Pinus, Cedrus). Leaves may be simple or compound; Cycas has pinnate leaves that last a few years.

Conifer needle-like leaves reduce surface area, and a thick cuticle and sunken stomata reduce water loss, helping them survive extremes of temperature, humidity and wind. Economic uses include timber, and products such as resin and turpentine from pines.

example.q: How do needle leaves help a Himalayan pine survive cold, dry winds?
steps: Needles have a small surface area, so less water is lost.
A thick cuticle cuts evaporation.
Sunken stomata lose less water.
example.answer: Small area, thick cuticle and sunken stomata reduce water loss.

learn.reallife: Deodar (Cedrus deodara) and chir pine forests of Himachal and Uttarakhand supply timber and resin; Cycas is a common ornamental in Indian gardens.

games.title: Gymnosperm facts
items: Gymnosperm ovules are enclosed in an ovary.
Ovules are exposed; there is no ovary wall.
Coralloid roots of Cycas fix nitrogen with the help of cyanobacteria.
They are associated with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria.
Seeds are not covered by a fruit wall.

quiz.q: 'Gymnosperm' literally means:
quiz.explain: Gymnos = naked, sperma = seed.

quiz.q: Coralloid roots are found in:
quiz.explain: Cycas has coralloid roots with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with mycorrhizal roots of Pinus

quiz.q: Mycorrhizal roots are seen in:
quiz.explain: Pinus roots associate with fungi as mycorrhizae.

quiz.q: Which adaptation of conifer leaves reduces water loss?
quiz.explain: Needles with thick cuticle and sunken stomata cut transpiration.
quiz.mistake: Picks features that increase water loss

quiz.q: In gymnosperms, the ovules are:
quiz.explain: Ovules are exposed before and after fertilisation.
options: Not enclosed by an ovary wall

quiz.q: Which gymnosperm is among the tallest tree species?
quiz.explain: Sequoia, the giant redwood, is one of the tallest trees.

quiz.q: The leaves of Cycas are:
quiz.explain: Cycas has large pinnate compound leaves that last several years.
options: Pinnate and persist for a few years

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Conifers can withstand extremes of temperature, humidity and wind. Reason (R): Conifer leaves are needle-like with a thick cuticle and sunken stomata.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; these leaf adaptations cut water loss and explain their tolerance.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect leaf structure to survival

quiz.q: Which of these is an economic use of gymnosperms such as pines and deodar?
quiz.explain: Conifers give timber, and pine resin is the source of turpentine. Agar and carrageen come from red algae; peat comes from the moss Sphagnum.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up products of algae and bryophytes with those of gymnosperms

teach.ask: Gappu hugs a pine tree: 'Why are its leaves like needles, and where are its seeds hiding?' Explain gymnosperms!
teach.praise: Chirp! Naked seeds and water-saving needles. Pines are tough!
teach.nudge: Good! Are gymnosperm seeds covered? And how do needles save water?

learn.hook: In spring, pine forests release clouds of yellow pollen. The wind carries it to female cones, and no water is needed at all.
points: Gymnosperms are heterosporous: haploid microspores and megaspores form in sporangia on sporophylls arranged spirally in strobili (cones).
Male strobili carry microsporophylls with microsporangia. Microspores develop into a highly reduced male gametophyte, the pollen grain, inside the microsporangium.

Female strobili carry megasporophylls with ovules. The ovule is the nucellus (megasporangium) protected by envelopes (integuments). A megaspore mother cell in the nucellus divides by meiosis into four megaspores; one forms the multicellular female gametophyte with two or more archegonia.

In Pinus, male and female cones are on the same tree; in Cycas, male cones and megasporophylls are on different trees. Male and female gametophytes are not free-living; they stay within sporangia on the sporophyte.

Pollen is carried by air to the ovule opening. A pollen tube carries male gametes to the archegonia. After fertilisation the zygote forms the embryo and the ovule becomes a seed, which is not covered.

example.q: Trace the path from microspore to seed in Pinus.
steps: Microspore develops into a pollen grain in the microsporangium.
Air carries pollen to an ovule on the female cone.
A pollen tube carries male gametes to the archegonia.
Fertilisation forms a zygote, which becomes the embryo.
The ovule develops into a naked seed.
example.answer: Microspore → pollen → pollination by air → pollen tube → fertilisation → embryo → naked seed.

learn.reallife: Pine pollen can coat cars yellow in Shimla in spring, a sign of wind pollination at work.

games.title: From pollen to seed
items: Pollen grain forms in the microsporangium
Air carries pollen to the ovule
Pollen tube grows towards the archegonia
Male gametes are released near the archegonium

games.title: Structure to meaning
pairs: Female sex organ in the female gametophyte

quiz.q: In gymnosperms, the male gametophyte is the:
quiz.explain: The highly reduced male gametophyte is the pollen grain.

quiz.q: Pollination in gymnosperms is mainly by:
quiz.explain: Pollen is carried by air currents to the ovules.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gymnosperms need water like ferns

quiz.q: The megaspore mother cell divides by meiosis to form how many megaspores?
quiz.explain: Meiosis of one megaspore mother cell gives four megaspores; one develops into the female gametophyte.
quiz.mistake: Confuses meiosis output with the number that survives

quiz.q: In which gymnosperm are male cones and megasporophylls borne on different trees?
quiz.explain: Cycas is dioecious; in Pinus both cones are on the same tree.

quiz.q: The female gametophyte of a gymnosperm bears:
quiz.explain: The multicellular female gametophyte bears two or more archegonia.
quiz.mistake: Places male organs in the ovule

quiz.q: Unlike bryophytes and pteridophytes, the gametophytes of gymnosperms:
quiz.explain: They remain within sporangia on the sporophyte.
options: Do not have an independent free-living existence

quiz.q: What carries male gametes to the archegonia in gymnosperms?
quiz.explain: The pollen tube carries male gametes, removing dependence on water.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Gymnosperms do not need water for fertilisation. Reason (R): The pollen tube delivers male gametes directly to the archegonia.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the pollen tube removes the need for gametes to swim through water.
quiz.mistake: Misses that the pollen tube is the reason

teach.ask: Gappu watches pine pollen blowing in the wind. 'How does that become a seed without any water?' Walk him through it!
teach.praise: Tweet! Pollen flies, a tube grows, gametes meet, and a naked seed forms. No swimming needed!
teach.nudge: Good! How do the male gametes reach the egg if there is no water?

topics.title: Comparing plant groups: from algae to gymnosperms

learn.hook: Imagine plants climbing a ladder out of the water: algae in the sea, mosses at the shore, ferns with pipes, pines with seeds, and flowering plants at the top.
points: Increasing complexity: algae → bryophytes → pteridophytes → gymnosperms → angiosperms. Angiosperms have ovules inside an ovary and seeds inside fruits.
Dominant phase: haploid gametophyte in bryophytes; diploid sporophyte in pteridophytes and gymnosperms.
Vascular tissue is absent in algae and bryophytes, present in pteridophytes and gymnosperms. Seeds appear first in gymnosperms (naked); angiosperm seeds are enclosed in fruits.
Water is needed for fertilisation in bryophytes and pteridophytes; gymnosperms use pollen tubes.

Ploidy check: moss protonema, leafy gametophyte, gemma cell, fern prothallus, spores and gametes are haploid (n); zygotes and sporophytes are diploid (2n). Algae are classified mainly by pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella.

example.q: Give the ploidy of: moss protonema cell, fern prothallus cell, zygote of fern, gemma cell of Marchantia.
steps: Protonema is part of the gametophyte: n.
Prothallus is the fern gametophyte: n.
Zygote forms by fusion of gametes: 2n.
Gemma is an asexual bud of the haploid thallus: n.

learn.reallife: In a typical Indian forest walk in the Western Ghats you can see the whole ladder in a day: algae in streams, mosses on rocks, ferns on banks, and cycads or pines planted nearby.

quiz.q: Which group was the first to produce seeds?
quiz.explain: Gymnosperms have seeds, though they are naked.
quiz.mistake: Credits heterosporous pteridophytes with true seeds

quiz.q: The dominant phase of a fern is the:
quiz.explain: In pteridophytes the sporophyte is dominant.

quiz.q: What is the ploidy of a cell of a moss protonema?
quiz.explain: The protonema is a gametophytic stage, so haploid.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every vegetative cell is diploid

quiz.q: Which feature distinguishes gymnosperms from angiosperms?
quiz.explain: Angiosperm ovules lie inside an ovary and seeds inside fruits; gymnosperm ovules and seeds are exposed.
options: Gymnosperm ovules are not enclosed in an ovary

quiz.q: Which plant group has vascular tissue but no seeds?
quiz.explain: Pteridophytes have xylem and phloem but reproduce by spores.

quiz.q: Algae are classified into classes mainly on the basis of:
quiz.explain: The three algal classes differ in pigments, food reserves, walls and flagella.
options: Pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella

quiz.q: Which plant group needs water for fertilisation?
quiz.explain: Pteridophytes (and bryophytes) have swimming antherozoids.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The fern prothallus is haploid. Reason (R): The fern prothallus develops from a spore produced by meiosis.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the spore is haploid, so the prothallus that grows from it by mitosis is haploid.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect meiosis with haploidy

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Moss, fern, pine: how do I tell which is more advanced?' Compare the groups for him!
teach.praise: Chirp! Gametophyte to sporophyte, no pipes to pipes, spores to seeds. The plant ladder!
teach.nudge: Good! Which group has the dominant gametophyte, and which first has seeds?
